stories.headline: World court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.question: What does the world court's genocide ruling against Myanmar actually change for the Rohingya?
stories.dek: For the first time, the world court has held a country responsible for genocide. Myanmar must stop, punish, allow safe return and plan compensation, but the court cannot force it to.

so_far.text: The Rohingya are a people of northern Rakhine State in Myanmar. A 1982 citizenship law left most of them stateless. In 2017 the army launched an offensive, and around 740,000 to 750,000 Rohingya fled. In November 2019 Gambia sued Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's top court for disputes between countries. Hearings on the main question ran for three weeks in January 2026.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026 the ICJ ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations. It found security forces killed thousands, committed widespread sexual violence, destroyed villages and imposed measures to prevent births. Myanmar also failed to prevent and punish genocide, and failed to preserve evidence as ordered in 2020. The court rejected Gambia's claim of direct public incitement. It is the first time the ICJ has held a state responsible for committing genocide.

steps.text: The Genocide Convention turns genocide into a broken treaty duty, so a member country can be judged on it.
Because every member shares that duty, Gambia could sue without any direct link to the crimes.
The court found killings, sexual violence, destroyed villages and birth prevention, and inferred intent to destroy from that pattern.
That makes Myanmar responsible as a state, bringing duties to stop, punish, allow safe return and plan compensation.
But the court has no police, so enforcement depends on the Security Council, the General Assembly and other countries.

history.text: The story begins with a treaty. The 1948 Genocide Convention binds its members not to commit genocide, and to prevent and punish it. In 1982 a Myanmar citizenship law left most Rohingya stateless, meaning no country counted them as citizens. An armed group, ARSA, formed in 2013. After ARSA attacks in 2017, the army launched an offensive, and around 740,000 to 750,000 Rohingya fled. In 2019 a UN fact-finding mission found 'genocidal acts'. In November 2019 Gambia, with no direct link to the crimes, sued using its Convention membership, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). Human Rights Watch says no country had done that before to bring such a case. In January 2020 the court ordered provisional measures, emergency orders that included preserving evidence. In February 2021 the military overthrew Aung San Suu Kyi's government; the civil war since has killed an estimated 100,000 people. ASEAN, the Southeast Asian bloc, first barred Myanmar's leader in 2021. In July 2022 the court rejected all of Myanmar's objections, so it could judge the main question. On 18 November 2026 Min Aung Hlaing, now president of an army-backed government, said Myanmar would review its ASEAN ties after the bloc again barred its senior leaders.

analogy.text: Think of a housing society whose members all sign one rulebook. If one member badly harms others, any member can complain to the society's tribunal, even one who was not hurt. The tribunal can rule that the member broke the rules and order repairs.
analogy.breaks: Unlike a society, this tribunal has no one to make the member pay. Members can only add pressure, and the Security Council has never stepped in.

for_you.text: The ruling changes no Indian law. Rohingya living in India face arbitrary detention and fear of deportation. India has no refugee law, and the Home Ministry calls them illegal immigrants. The court ordered Myanmar to allow safe, voluntary return, but it is not yet known whether that will affect how India treats Rohingya here.

misconception.myth: The ruling means Myanmar's generals will now be tried and jailed.
misconception.fact: The ruling holds Myanmar, the state, responsible; it prosecutes no one. Individuals are a matter for the ICC, where judges have not ruled on a warrant for Min Aung Hlaing.

next.text: Myanmar must report on a compensation plan by November 2028. Gambia could take the judgment to the UN Security Council, which has never enforced an ICJ ruling. ICC judges have yet to rule on the arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing.

lesson.concept: How a world court holds a country responsible
lesson.big_idea: When countries sign a treaty, they take on duties. Any member can ask the world court to rule that another broke them. The court can declare it and order remedies, but cannot enforce them.

steps.title: A treaty creates duties
steps.text: Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, member countries promise not to commit genocide, and to prevent and punish it. Each promise can be broken separately, so the court rules on each.

steps.title: Any member can sue
steps.text: Because all members share these duties, any member can take another to the ICJ. Gambia had no direct link to the crimes but sued as a member.

steps.title: Proving acts and intent
steps.text: Genocide needs harmful acts against a group plus intent to destroy that group. Intent is rarely written down, so the court can infer it from a pattern of conduct.

steps.title: The state, not people
steps.text: The ICJ rules on whether a country broke its duties. It jails no one. Individuals are tried at a separate court, the International Criminal Court (ICC).

steps.title: Final, but not self-enforcing
steps.text: The judgment cannot be appealed, but the ICJ has no police. The winner can turn to the UN Security Council, which has never enforced an ICJ judgment, or to pressure.

example.setup: Imagine Country A and faraway Country B both signed the Genocide Convention. A's army attacks a minority group inside A. B was not harmed itself, but decides to act.

lines.label: Stage 1: B sues
lines.calc: B files at the court as a treaty member
lines.note: No direct link needed; membership is enough.

lines.label: Stage 2: urgent orders
lines.calc: Court orders A to protect the group, keep evidence
lines.note: Provisional measures apply while the case continues.

lines.label: Stage 3: objections
lines.calc: A says the court can't hear it; rejected
lines.note: Only then does the court reach the main question.

lines.label: Stage 4: the vote
lines.calc: Assume 15 judges: 8 needed; 9 say genocide
lines.note: A majority decides, and there is no appeal.

lines.label: Stage 5: remedies
lines.calc: Stop, punish, allow return, plan compensation
lines.note: Duties on the state, not jail terms for people.

lines.label: Stage 6: A refuses
lines.calc: B goes to Security Council or builds pressure
lines.note: The court itself cannot force A to comply.

example.result: The ruling settles who broke the law and what duties follow. Whether those duties are carried out depends on other countries, not on the court.

apply.text: Myanmar's case followed these stages: Gambia sued in November 2019, the court ordered provisional measures in January 2020, rejected Myanmar's objections in July 2022, and ruled 9–6 on 19 November 2026. Myanmar must now report on compensation by November 2028. If it refuses, Gambia's routes are the Security Council, which has never enforced an ICJ judgment, the General Assembly, or pressure from states.

practice.q: Suppose Country A loses but ignores the order to plan compensation. Can A appeal, and what can Country B do next?
practice.answer: Step 1: The judgment is final, so A cannot appeal. Step 2: The court has no police, so it cannot force A. Step 3: B can take the judgment to the UN Security Council. Step 4: Since the Council has never done this, B may also seek General Assembly and state pressure.

terms.meaning: International Court of Justice: the UN's top court, judging disputes between countries.
International Criminal Court: tries individual people for crimes such as genocide.
1948 treaty: members must not commit genocide, and must prevent and punish it.
Emergency orders a court gives to protect people while a case continues.

check.q: Why does this ruling not, by itself, put Min Aung Hlaing on trial?
options: Because the vote was only nine to six
Because the ICJ judges states, while individuals are tried at a separate court, the ICC
Because Myanmar can still appeal the judgment
check.why: The ICJ decides state responsibility. Individual guilt is for the ICC. A majority is enough, and the judgment cannot be appealed.

takeaways: The world court judges countries, not people; its rulings are final but not self-enforcing.
On 19 November 2026 it found Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a first for any state.

stories.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi agree on nuclear risk, not Ukraine
stories.question: What did Trump, Putin and Xi agree in Shenzhen, and what does it mean for Ukraine?
stories.dek: A joint declaration says nuclear war must never be fought, but sets no arms limits and no Ukraine terms. Ukraine talks continue separately, and no date is set for the next round.

so_far.text: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In 2026 Russia demands the Donbas region as the price of peace; Ukraine is reluctant to give up land. Talks in Abu Dhabi the week before the summit were the first in nine months. On 16–17 November a Ukrainian strike collapsed a road arch of the Crimean Bridge, a vital supply line for Russian troops. Zelensky called it a reply to Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026 Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping held their first-ever three-way meeting, for about 80 minutes in Shenzhen. They issued a joint declaration: nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and the three will hold talks on reducing nuclear risks and stopping the spread of nuclear weapons. It sets no arms limits and names no Ukraine terms. It also backs UN reform and more refined-petroleum supply, and warns the International Criminal Court (ICC), which wants Putin, against abusing its powers. China and Russia released identical texts; the US had not published its own. Trump and Putin met for about 40 minutes.

steps.text: A joint declaration states shared principles; it fixes no numbers, borders or deadlines that anyone must meet.
So the three leaders agreed on easy ground, that nuclear war is unwinnable, and left arms limits out.
Ukraine's war turns on land: Russia demands Donbas, and Ukraine is reluctant to give it up.
Ukraine talks run separately: Berlin covered security guarantees, and Kushner says Russia agreed to a format including Europe.
Fighting runs alongside the talks: the Crimean Bridge, a key Russian supply line, was attacked on 16–17 and 19 November.

history.text: The root of this story is 2014. In February unmarked Russian troops took Crimea, and in March Russia annexed it. On 19 March 2014 Putin announced a bridge to Crimea. In April Russian-backed militants seized towns in Donbas, starting the Donbas war. The Minsk II agreements of February 2015 were meant to settle that war but were never fully implemented, so the conflict stayed open. The bridge opened to cars in May 2018, cost about $3.7 billion, and became a vital supply line for Russian troops. In February 2022 Russia launched its full-scale invasion, and in September 2022 it declared four more Ukrainian provinces annexed. The bridge was then hit in October 2022, in July 2023, when two people were killed, and in June 2025 with underwater explosives. In August 2024 Ukraine's Kursk incursion became its first major ground offensive into Russia. By 2026 the core dispute is land: Russia demands Donbas for peace, and Ukraine is reluctant to cede territory.

lesson.concept: How a security guarantee deters an attack
lesson.big_idea: A security guarantee is a promise that other countries will help defend one country if it is attacked. It works by making an attack look too costly, but only if the attacker believes the promise.

steps.title: A promise to defend
steps.text: A security guarantee is a promise by other countries to help defend one country if it is attacked. Its main job is to stop the attack from ever starting.

steps.title: Article 5: one for all
steps.text: The best-known model is Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty. An armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all. Each member then takes the action it judges necessary, which can include armed force.

steps.title: Deterrence is a sum
steps.text: Deterrence means making an attack look too costly to try. An attacker adds up what it would face: the target's own forces plus everyone who promised to help. A bigger total means a less tempting attack.

steps.title: Only believed help counts
steps.text: The attacker counts only help it believes will really come. Vague wording weakens that belief. For Ukraine, outside NATO, the talk is of 'Article 5-style' guarantees, and their form is still unclear.

example.setup: Imagine a small country with 100 tanks next to a bigger neighbour with 300. Four friendly countries each promise 100 tanks if it is attacked. All numbers are made up.

lines.label: Alone
lines.calc: 100 tanks vs 300 tanks
lines.note: The attacker has three times as many.

lines.label: Promised help
lines.calc: 4 friends × 100 = 400 tanks
lines.note: Counts only if the attacker believes they will come.

lines.label: With the guarantee
lines.note: Now the attacker is outnumbered.

lines.label: Attacker's decision
lines.calc: 500 vs 300: attack looks too risky
lines.note: The guarantee works before a shot is fired.

example.result: The promise turns a three-to-one disadvantage into a five-to-three advantage, so the attack looks far riskier. But the sum holds only if the attacker believes the four friends will come.

apply.text: The Shenzhen declaration names no Ukraine terms, so it does not touch this sum. The guarantee is being discussed elsewhere: Berlin talks covered post-war security guarantees. Kushner says Russia is comfortable with Article 5-style guarantees, but the form is unclear and Russia has not commented. Macron urged reopening the question of NATO entry.

practice.q: Same country, but the attacker believes only two of the four friends would really come. How does the sum look now?
practice.answer: Count only believed help: 2 × 100 = 200 tanks. Add the country's own 100: 300 tanks. Against 300 attacking tanks, the sides are now even, not five to three. A doubted promise deters far less, which is why the form of Ukraine's guarantee matters.

stories.headline: Iran strikes Kuwait and Bahrain bases, yet oil prices ease
stories.question: Is the Iran war spreading across the Gulf, and what does it mean for oil?
stories.dek: Attacks reached Kuwait, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia's capital but did little damage. Oil still eased, because the IEA says world supply now exceeds demand. Prices remain far above pre-war levels.

so_far.text: The war began on 28 February 2026, when the US and Israel struck Iran. Iran then blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea exit from the Gulf, and targeted tankers. The US in turn blockades Iran's ports. In mid-November Iran attacked a US radar installation in Bahrain. On 17 November the US answered by striking a Revolutionary Guard missile-launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island. The new attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain followed that strike.

what_happened.text: On 18 November Iran said it targeted the US Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. Kuwait said its air defences intercepted the drones, with no immediate damage. Bahrain, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet, intercepted several Iranian attacks and reported no damage or casualties. Separately, Houthi missiles hit the Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh, damaging several floors; Saudi authorities reported no injuries. On 19 November the International Energy Agency (IEA) called the crisis the largest threat to energy security in history. Yet Brent crude settled at about $91.98 a barrel that day.

steps.text: Iran attacked a US radar in Bahrain, so the US struck a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island on 17 November.
Iran replied on 18 November against US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, Gulf states that host American forces.
Air defences intercepted the drones, so damage stayed small, but Houthi missiles still damaged a Riyadh tower.
Oil barely reacted, because the IEA says world supply now exceeds demand for the first time since the war began.
That surplus cushions prices, but the IEA says consumers increasingly pay through high prices as other buffers run down.

history.text:
The root is February 2026, when the US and Israel struck Iran. Iran answered by blockading the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow exit from the Gulf, and targeting tankers. Before the crisis, about one-fifth of world oil shipments passed through Hormuz, so the shock was global. Brent crude, the main world oil price, rose from about $72 before the war to about $125 by late April.

The US then blockaded Iran's ports to cut its oil sales, which put crews in danger. In June 2026 US strikes on Indian-crewed tankers killed three Indian seafarers on the Settebello. India summoned the US chargé d'affaires, the embassy's acting head. US Central Command said the ship was moving Iranian oil against the blockade. On 14 July the UAE said Iranian missiles hit two tankers in Hormuz, killing one sailor.

The war also divided Washington. In September the US House passed a measure to limit Trump's Iran war powers, 220 to 204. From mid-October Iran claimed several tankers had hit mines; none was independently verified. Brent was still about $115 on 28 October. In mid-November a new cycle of strike and reply began: Iran hit a US radar in Bahrain, and the US struck Qeshm Island on 17 November.

lesson.concept: Why oil prices can fall during a war
lesson.big_idea: Oil's price follows the balance between barrels on offer and barrels wanted. A war cuts supply and prices jump, but if demand falls and other supply rises, prices can fall mid-war.

steps.title: Price follows a balance
steps.text: Supply is the barrels on offer; demand is the barrels buyers want. If buyers want more than is on offer, that is a shortfall and prices rise. If more is on offer, that is a surplus and prices fall.

steps.title: A war cuts supply
steps.text: Blocking a route removes barrels. About one-fifth of world oil shipments passed through Hormuz before the crisis, so blocking it opened a big shortfall. Brent rose from about $72 to about $125 by late April.

steps.title: High prices change behaviour
steps.text: Expensive oil makes buyers use less and draws extra barrels from elsewhere, such as other sellers or stockpiles. Over months, demand shrinks and supply grows, closing the gap.

steps.title: A surplus pulls prices down
steps.text: Once supply exceeds demand, prices fall even while the war continues. The IEA says this has now happened for the first time since the war began.

steps.title: Someone still pays
steps.text: A surplus reached through high prices means people cut back and buffers run down. The IEA says consumers increasingly absorb the impact, and some places face shortfalls.

example.setup: Imagine a small world where buyers want 100 barrels a day and sellers supply exactly 100. Then a war blocks 20 barrels a day. Assume all numbers.

lines.label: Before the war
lines.calc: Supply 100 = demand 100
lines.note: Balanced, so the price is steady.

lines.label: War blocks 20
lines.note: Buyers still want 100.

lines.label: The shortfall
lines.calc: 100 − 80 = 20 barrels short
lines.note: Buyers bid against each other, so the price jumps.

lines.label: Demand falls
lines.calc: Assume demand drops from 100 to 90
lines.note: Expensive oil makes buyers use less.

lines.label: Others add 15
lines.calc: Assume supply: 80 + 15 = 95
lines.note: High prices pull in extra barrels from elsewhere.

lines.label: The surplus
lines.calc: 95 − 90 = 5 spare barrels
lines.note: Spare oil, so the price falls despite the war.

example.result: The 20 blocked barrels never came back, yet the market swung from 20 short to 5 spare, so prices fall. The hidden cost: buyers now use 10 fewer barrels a day.

apply.text: That is Brent's story. Losing Hormuz pushed it to about $125 in late April. Now the IEA says supply exceeds demand, so Brent settled near $91.98 on 19 November even after attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain. But it is still far above the pre-war $72, and the IEA warns consumers are paying through high prices.

practice.q: Same small world: supply 95, demand 90. A new attack blocks 8 more barrels a day. Surplus or shortfall, and which way does the price lean?
practice.answer: New supply: 95 − 8 = 87. Demand is still 90. 90 − 87 = 3 barrels short. That is a shortfall, so the price leans up again. An attack moves prices most when it tips the balance.

stories.headline: Israeli troops cross Gaza's Yellow Line for first time since truce
stories.question: Why has Israel sent troops beyond Gaza's Yellow Line, and is the ceasefire collapsing?
stories.dek: Israel says it targeted a tunnel that threatened its troops. Hamas calls the raid a flagrant violation. The short raid exposes a stuck deal that the Board of Peace says could collapse.

so_far.text: A ceasefire based on Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan took effect on 10 October 2025. In phase one, Israeli troops pulled back to a boundary called the Yellow Line, still holding about 53% of Gaza. Phase two was announced on 14 January 2026. It covers disarming Hamas, an international stabilisation force and a technocratic administration. It has stalled. Al Jazeera reports that Hamas agreed in July to a roadmap to give up weapons and governance, but Israel rejected it. Israel has since moved the Yellow Line, which now covers roughly two-thirds of Gaza.

what_happened.text: On 18 November 2026, Israeli tanks and ground forces crossed the Yellow Line into central Gaza near Nuseirat. NBC News reports it was the first such operation beyond the line since the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel said the aim was to dismantle a tunnel that posed an 'immediate and direct threat' to its troops. On 19 November the Israeli military said the operation had ended. Medics reported at least one person killed in an Israeli airstrike near the raid; another report said three. Gaza's Hamas-run media office said about 6,000 people fled their homes and tents. Hamas called the raid a 'flagrant' ceasefire violation.

steps.text: Phase one froze the fighting along the Yellow Line, leaving Israeli troops holding about 53% of Gaza.
Phase two stalled: Israel rejected Hamas's July roadmap and has not let the technocratic administration start, which holds up the stabilisation force.
With no next step, Israel kept moving the line, and Israel Katz says Israel won't withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel says Hamas tunnels and ceasefire violations threaten its troops, so it presents raids like this one as removing threats.
Hamas calls this a flagrant violation, and the Board of Peace warns the whole deal could collapse.

history.text:
The story's roots go back two decades. In 2005 Israel withdrew from Gaza. In 2006 the militant group Hamas won Palestinian elections, and in 2007 it seized Gaza. Israel and Egypt then imposed a blockade on Gaza.

On 7 October 2023 Hamas attacked Israel, which started the Gaza war. Two truces followed, and both ended. The first ran from 24 November to 1 December 2023. The second began on 19 January 2025 and collapsed when Israel resumed attacks on 18 March 2025. So every pause so far has been temporary.

On 29 September 2025 Donald Trump announced a peace plan. It took effect on 10 October 2025. Israeli forces pulled back to the Yellow Line before hostages were released. On 17 November 2025 the UN Security Council endorsed the plan in Resolution 2803, giving it international backing. In late 2025, 100 to 200 Hamas fighters were reported trapped in tunnels on the Israeli-held side of the line. Israel's defence minister said destroying tunnels was central to its mission there.

On 14 January 2026 Steve Witkoff announced phase two. It covers disarming Hamas, an international stabilisation force, technocratic governance and the Board of Peace. On 21 January Trump demanded that Hamas disarm. Phase two then stalled, and the Yellow Line stayed in place. That set the stage for the raid of 18 November 2026.

lesson.concept: How a phased ceasefire is meant to work
lesson.big_idea: A phased ceasefire takes hard steps in order: first stop shooting and pull back, later settle weapons and who governs. If the later phase stalls, the temporary first-phase line starts to look permanent.

steps.title: Phase one: freeze and pull back
steps.text: Fighting stops and troops withdraw to an agreed line. In Gaza, Israeli forces pulled back to the Yellow Line before hostages were released, still holding about 53% of Gaza.

steps.title: Phase two: the hard questions
steps.text: The second stage tackles what was too hard at first: weapons and who runs things. Gaza's phase two covers Hamas disarmament, an international stabilisation force, a technocratic administration (run by non-political experts) and the Board of Peace.

steps.title: Each step depends on another
steps.text: The steps are linked like a chain. In Gaza, Israel has not let the technocratic administration start, which holds up the stabilisation force. Israel Katz says Israel won't withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.

steps.title: A stalled chain freezes the line
steps.text: If the chain stops, the 'temporary' line stays, and the side holding it can shift it. Israel has gradually moved the Yellow Line, which now covers roughly two-thirds of Gaza.

steps.title: Raids test the edges
steps.text: Each side then accuses the other of breaking the truce. Violations pile up until people ask whether the deal still exists, which is what the Board of Peace now warns about.

example.setup: Imagine two villages fighting over a 100-acre field. A mediator gets them to stop. Village A's guards pull back to a painted line, but still hold 53 acres.

lines.label: Phase one done
lines.calc: A holds 53 of 100 acres
lines.note: Shooting stops; A's guards stay behind the painted line.

lines.label: Phase two needs
lines.calc: B hands in weapons; neutral managers arrive
lines.note: Both must happen, and each side wants the other to move first.

lines.label: The deadlock
lines.calc: B offers a roadmap; A rejects it
lines.note: A wants B disarmed before anything else, so nothing moves.

lines.label: Line drifts
lines.calc: 53 → 67 acres, about two-thirds of the field
lines.note: A moves the paint, step by step.

lines.label: A raid across
lines.calc: A's guards cross to fill a ditch
lines.note: A calls it removing a threat; B calls it a violation.

example.result: With phase two stuck, the 'temporary' line kept growing, and each crossing deepens mistrust. The deal survives on paper, but there is less and less to return to.

apply.text: That is Gaza now. Phase one left Israel at the Yellow Line, holding about 53% of Gaza. Phase two stalled when Israel rejected Hamas's July roadmap. The line grew to roughly two-thirds, and on 18 November 2026 troops crossed it near Nuseirat. The Board of Peace warns there may be 'no road map to return to'.

practice.q: Suppose the field is 200 acres. Village A first held 53% of it, and later two-thirds. How many extra acres did A take?
practice.answer: Start: 53% of 200 = 106 acres. Later: two-thirds of 200 is about 133 acres. Extra: 133 − 106 = about 27 acres, taken while phase two never started.

stories.headline: Bangladesh shutdown by Hasina's banned party turns violent in 28 districts
stories.question: Why is Bangladesh's violence getting worse, and where does India fit in?
stories.dek: Hasina's banned party escalated after she was refused a passport while in exile in India. PM Tarique Rahman warned of conspiracies. Headlines say he blamed India, but the text we read doesn't name India.

so_far.text: Bangladesh is governed by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. Its old rival, Sheikh Hasina's Awami League, is banned from political activity and was barred from the election. Hasina lives in exile in India. In early November 2026 the government blamed her for garment-factory unrest. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed alleged that factory owners linked to the Awami League were involved. Workers want a minimum wage of Tk 30,000 a month, up from Tk 12,500. After party leaders were arrested, Awami League and Chhatra League activists attacked Tungipara police station in Gopalganj on 17 November.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026 Awami League supporters enforced a nationwide shutdown that turned violent in at least 28 districts. Former interim leader Muhammad Yunus's ancestral home in Chattogram was set on fire. A highway linking Dhaka and Gopalganj was hit. Several police and civilians were hurt; no figures were given. Police reported two members of the ruling BNP killed; one source says they died in Narail on 18 November. Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) sent 97 platoons to seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur. Rahman urged unity against 'conspiracies by defeated political forces'. Reuters and Telegraph India headlines say he blamed India. The agency text does not name India.

steps.text: The Awami League is banned and was barred from the election, so its supporters have no legal path to power.
The refusal of Hasina's passport and ID card blocked her route home and fed a week of rallies.
Arrests of party leaders set off the Tungipara attack, and the 19 November shutdown spread violence to 28 districts.

history.text:
The story starts in July 2024. Students were protesting job quotas, and they grew angrier after Hasina linked them to 'Razakars' on 14 July. Chhatra League attacks followed. Police shot a student, Abu Sayed, on 16 July, and the internet was shut on 18–19 July. The UN says the crackdown killed up to 1,400 people.

On 5 August 2024 Hasina resigned and fled to India. Mobs attacked Awami League offices, the homes of its MPs, and police stations. The party that had ruled the country became the target.

Three days later Muhammad Yunus took charge of an interim government. It banned the Awami League's activities and barred the party from the election. That closed its legal path to power.

On 23 December 2024 Dhaka first formally asked India to extradite Hasina, meaning hand her over. On 17 November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia, meaning without her being present. She called it a rigged tribunal. India said it noted the verdict and would 'engage constructively'. It later said it was examining the request. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera called extradition highly unlikely.

Before the 19 November 2026 shutdown, the government refused Hasina a new passport and national ID card, which she says she needs to come home. That refusal fed a week of Awami League rallies.

lesson.concept: How extradition between two countries works
lesson.big_idea: When a wanted person is in another country, the home country can only ask for them back. The host country decides under its own laws and treaties, and nobody can force it.

steps.title: A request, not an order
steps.text: Extradition means one country formally asking another to hand over a wanted person. The request goes through diplomats. Dhaka sent its first formal request for Hasina to India on 23 December 2024.

steps.title: The host checks the rules
steps.text: The host country checks its treaty and its own laws. Two common tests: is the act a crime in both countries, and is the case really criminal rather than political? Exact rules differ by treaty.

steps.title: Courts, then government, decide
steps.text: In many countries a court first checks the legal tests and the evidence. The government then makes the final call, weighing the law, the fairness of the trial, and relations with the asking country.

steps.title: Waiting is also a decision
steps.text: There is usually no deadline that forces an answer. A host can keep 'examining' a request for a long time. India has said it was examining the request for Hasina.

steps.title: Delay can strain relations
steps.text: While the person stays, relations between the two countries can suffer. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera said Hasina's extradition was highly unlikely and that this could strain already poor ties.

example.setup: Imagine Country A convicts its former leader in absentia. She is living in Country B. Country A wants her back to serve the sentence.

lines.label: Stage 1: The request
lines.calc: A sends B a formal extradition request
lines.note: Sent through diplomats, citing the conviction.

lines.label: Stage 2: Legal tests
lines.calc: Crime in both countries? Political case? Assume both tests apply
lines.note: The treaty sets the tests; here we assume them.

lines.label: Stage 3: Court review
lines.calc: B's court checks evidence and trial fairness
lines.note: A trial without the accused present can raise fairness questions.

lines.label: Stage 4: Government call
lines.calc: B's ministers: hand over, refuse, or wait
lines.note: Law and diplomacy both weigh here.

lines.label: Stage 5: The fallout
lines.calc: B waits; ties between A and B strain
lines.note: Nobody can force B to act.

example.result: Country A can ask but cannot compel. As long as Country B waits, the former leader stays where she is, and relations between the two countries can sour.

apply.text: Bangladesh is Country A and India is Country B. Dhaka asked for Hasina on 23 December 2024, and India said it was examining the request. She is still in India, and Dhaka refused her a new passport. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera called extradition highly unlikely and said it could strain ties. Headlines say Rahman blamed India; the agency text doesn't name India.

practice.q: Suppose Country B refuses outright, saying the case is political. What happens to the former leader, and what can Country A still do?
practice.answer: Step 1: the refusal ends the request in B's system, so she stays in B. Step 2: A cannot force her return. Step 3: A can only press diplomatically or ask again with new grounds. Relations would likely get worse.

check.q: Dhaka asked India to hand over Hasina in December 2024. Why is she still in India?

check.why: Extradition is only a request. India said it was examining it, and nothing forces a host country to answer by a deadline.

stories.headline: Malaysia ends visa-free entry for Indians from 1 January 2027
stories.question: Why is Malaysia ending visa-free entry for Indians, and what will travellers need now?
stories.dek: From 1 January 2027, Indians need a visa before flying to Malaysia. They can apply on MyVISA from 1 December 2026. Malaysia gave no reason, but India had warned about job-scam arrivals.

so_far.text: Since 1 December 2023, Indians could visit Malaysia for up to 30 days without a visa. They only had to register for the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card. In December 2024, shortly before the offer was due to expire, Malaysia extended it to the end of 2026. Arrivals from India grew fast, to about 1.4 million in 2025. In September 2026, India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur warned that more Indians were arriving on the facility, misled by agents with false job promises.

what_happened.text: Malaysia's Immigration Department issued a notice dated 17 November 2026. It says the visa exemption for Indian nationals will no longer be available from 1 January 2027. From then, Indians must get a valid visa before arriving. Applications open on Malaysia's MyVISA portal from 1 December 2026. Processing fees cannot be refunded, whatever the outcome, even if the policy or your plans change. The notice gives no reason. PTI reported it on 19 November, as did The Hindu and NDTV. The department says it can change entry rules at any time.

steps.text: Visa-free entry meant no check before travel. An officer decided only at the airport, with the traveller already there.
That made Malaysia easy to reach: Indian arrivals passed one million in 2024 and reached about 1.4 million in 2025.
India's High Commission said more Indians were arriving on the facility, misled by agents promising jobs that did not exist.
Malaysia promised in 2023 to curb overstaying. A visa lets it review each traveller before they fly.
But Malaysia's notice gives no official reason, so the link to these warnings is not confirmed.

history.text:
The story begins in late November 2023. Malaysia's home minister said the country would act to prevent overstaying by visa-free tourists from China and India. On 1 December 2023, a 30-day visa exemption for Indians began. Indians no longer applied for a visa. They only registered for the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card.

Travel jumped. Indian arrivals passed one million in 2024, up 71.7% on 2023. Malaysia's Immigration Director-General said visa-free entry lifted Indian tourist arrivals by 223%. In December 2024, shortly before it was due to expire, Malaysia extended the exemption to the end of 2026.

Visa-free never meant automatic entry. In 2025 some Indians were refused at the border for lacking return tickets, accommodation proof or enough funds. Arrivals still grew, to about 1.4 million that year.

In September 2026, India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur warned of a noticeable rise in Indians arriving on the facility, misled by agents with false job promises. It said the facility is for tourism and social visits only. Two months later, Malaysia's Immigration Department issued the notice ending the exemption.

lesson.concept: How a visa adds a check before travel
lesson.big_idea: Every country checks who comes in. Visa-free entry checks you only at the airport. A visa adds a check before you travel, which costs time and money but screens people earlier.

steps.title: Every entry gets checked
steps.text: When you land abroad, an immigration officer decides whether you may enter. They look at your passport, your reason for visiting, and whether you will leave on time.

steps.title: Visa-free: check at the door
steps.text: Under visa-free entry, you skip any application and simply fly. Indians could stay up to 30 days this way. But officers could still refuse: in 2025 some Indians were refused for lacking return tickets, accommodation proof or funds.

steps.title: Visa: an extra check first
steps.text: With a visa, you apply in advance and the government reviews you while you are at home. Officers usually still check you on arrival. From 1 January 2027, Indians need a valid visa before arriving, applied for on MyVISA from 1 December 2026.

steps.title: The check has a cost
steps.text: Each application takes time and a fee. Malaysia's processing fees are non-refundable whatever the outcome, even if plans or policy change. The exact amount for Indians is not officially confirmed.

steps.title: Why a country switches
steps.text: Checking earlier lets officials screen a traveller's purpose before arrival. That matters if people use tourist entry to look for work, as India's High Commission warned in September 2026.

apply.text: That is the switch Malaysia is making. From 1 January 2027, every Indian traveller faces an earlier check on the MyVISA portal before flying. Officers at the airport usually still have the final say. Malaysia gave no reason, but a visa lets it screen people before they fly, including the job-seekers India's High Commission warned about in September 2026.

practice.q: A couple plans a 2027 trip. Assume visas cost ₹2,500 each. They apply, get visas, then cancel the trip. How much do they lose?
practice.answer: Two visas: 2 × ₹2,500 = ₹5,000. Malaysia's fees are non-refundable, even if travel plans change, so the refund is ₹0. They lose ₹5,000, money a 2026 trip under the exemption would not have cost.

stories.headline: Anthropic's record IPO opens 34% up, closes 17% higher
stories.question: How did Anthropic's record IPO trade on day one, and is AI a bubble?
stories.dek: Shares opened 34% above the $83 IPO price on 19 November and closed 17% up. That shows strong demand for few shares, not proven profits. Analysts split; Europe's central bank warns on AI debt.

so_far.text: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant, set the price for its IPO (its first sale of shares to the public) at $83 per share on 18 November 2026. That was above its planned range of $70–$78. Trading on the Nasdaq exchange was set to start on 19 November. At $83, the company was valued at about $1.5 trillion counting every share that could exist, or about $1.03 trillion on shares already issued, according to The Hindu. On 18 November the European Central Bank also published a warning about AI debt.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026, Anthropic's shares began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. CBS News says they opened at $111.50, about 34% above the $83 IPO price; another report put the first trade near $110. They touched a high of $114.99, when the company's value topped $2 trillion. Then gains shrank, and ANT closed at $97.17, up about 17%. CBC reported the Nasdaq index fell the same day. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion, the largest IPO ever, beating SpaceX's $75 billion. A $26 billion private placement takes the total to about $107 billion.

steps.text: Only about 7.4% of Anthropic's shares trade publicly, so few shares were available for many eager buyers.
When many buyers chase few shares, they bid the price up; ANT opened at $111.50, 34% above $83.
The gains shrank during the day; ANT closed at $97.17, still about 17% above the IPO price.
A share price is a bet on future profits; Anthropic is unprofitable, with about $6.2 billion of debt and nearly $1 trillion in commitments.
The ECB says AI building is increasingly debt-funded, so a shift in mood could spread losses from shares to bond markets.

history.text: Anthropic was incorporated in January 2021 by former OpenAI staff, including Dario and Daniela Amodei. It released its AI assistant, Claude, in March 2023. Training such models costs huge sums, so the company needed rich backers. Amazon began investing in September 2023, with $1.25 billion and a promise of up to $4 billion. Google followed from October 2023. By November 2024, Amazon had doubled its total to $8 billion. These deals turned a young start-up into a company backed by two of the biggest tech firms. Investors then paid ever higher prices for a slice. Anthropic's private valuation is the price set in private funding rounds, where only big investors can buy. It went from $61.5 billion in March 2025 to $183 billion in September 2025, $380 billion in February 2026 and $965 billion in May 2026. That is more than fifteen times higher in about fourteen months. In June 2026 SpaceX raised $75 billion, then the largest IPO ever. On 18 November 2026 Anthropic priced its own IPO at $83, opening its shares to everyone, including retail investors, who were to get up to 20% of the offer.

lesson.concept: How an IPO's first-day 'pop' is measured
lesson.big_idea: In an IPO, a company sells new shares at one fixed price and keeps that money. Once trading starts, the market sets a new price. The gap is the 'pop', and it goes to buyers, not the company.

steps.title: The company fixes one price
steps.text: Before trading starts, the company and its bankers set one IPO price for every new share sold. Anthropic set $83 on 18 November 2026, above its planned $70–$78 range.

steps.title: It keeps that money
steps.text: The company receives the IPO price for each new share. Price times shares sold equals the money raised. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion this way, the largest IPO ever.

steps.title: Then the market sets prices
steps.text: Once trading opens, buyers and sellers agree prices on the exchange, second by second. If few shares are on offer and many people want them, the price rises. Only about 7.4% of Anthropic's shares trade publicly.

steps.title: The pop is a percentage
steps.text: The pop measures the rise against the IPO price: (trading price − IPO price) ÷ IPO price × 100. You can measure it at the open, at the day's high, or at the close.

steps.title: The gain goes to buyers
steps.text: Whoever bought at the IPO price now holds shares worth more. This 'paper gain' becomes real only when they sell. The company already has its money, so the gap is often called 'money left on the table'.

example.setup: Say a small company sells 1,000 new shares in its IPO at ₹100 each. On day one, the price opens at ₹134 and closes at ₹117.

lines.label: Money raised
lines.note: The company keeps this, and only this.

lines.label: Pop at the open
lines.note: Always measured against the IPO price.

lines.label: Pop at the close
lines.note: Gains shrank, but the price is still above ₹100.

lines.label: Buyers' paper gain
lines.note: Belongs to the buyers; real only if they sell.

example.result: The company raised ₹1 lakh whatever happened next. The 17% pop at the close gave its first buyers ₹17,000 on paper: money the company left on the table.

apply.text: Anthropic followed the same pattern. It priced at $83 and raised $81.3 billion. ANT opened at $111.50, a 34% pop, and closed at $97.17, a 17% pop. Those gains belong to buyers who got $83 shares, including the chip and cloud firms in the $26 billion placement, not to Anthropic.

practice.q: Same company: 1,000 shares sold at ₹100. Suppose a year later the price is ₹50. What is the change, and does the company lose its ₹1 lakh?
practice.answer: Change = (₹50 − ₹100) ÷ ₹100 = −50%. The buyers' shares fall from ₹1,00,000 to ₹50,000, a ₹50,000 paper loss. The company still keeps its ₹1,00,000; the loss falls on whoever holds the shares.

stories.headline: Trump rejects global AI rules as California and Europe act
stories.question: Who will set the rules for powerful AI now that Trump rejects global regulation?
stories.dek: On 19 November Trump told APEC the US opposes 'globalist' AI regulation. So rules are coming place by place instead, from California, the EU and Australia, as safety warnings grow.

so_far.text: Through 2026, governments grew worried that powerful AI could be misused or slip out of human control. In July the European Commission said it was in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic about AI-linked hacking incidents. On 10 November Australia announced six mandatory AI protections. On 16 November California's Attorney General sued OpenAI, alleging deception, obstruction and more than 80 loss-of-control incidents in testing.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026, at APEC in Shenzhen, China, US President Donald Trump said the US opposes 'any form of globalist regulation or anything to control and stifle' superintelligence. 'We won't allow that to happen,' he said, while adding 'we have to watch it'. He spoke before a planned meeting with Xi Jinping, where AI was expected to come up. On 18 November Newsom's office proposed mandatory AI safety standards, and a US watchdog's chatbot tests were reported. On 19 November an EU official said an AI cyberattack targeted the EU in October.

steps.text: Binding global rules need the big AI powers to agree, and the US refused at Paris in 2025 and again at APEC.
So each government writes rules for its own territory: the EU AI Act, Australia's protections, California's proposals.
Fresh warnings add pressure: GAO found four major chatbots produced viable attack plans in under 12 hours.
Politico calls California's plan a 'template' for Washington, and Newsom's office says it is 'getting even stronger'.
Companies selling worldwide must obey each market's binding rules, so the strictest big markets can shape AI everywhere.

history.text:
The root is February 2025. At the AI Action Summit in Paris, 58 countries signed a joint declaration. The US did not. Vice President JD Vance warned that excessive regulation 'could kill a transformative sector'. That set the US line against a shared global rulebook.

Others went their own way. On 5 November 2025 India's IT ministry, MeitY, issued AI Governance Guidelines. They are voluntary and light-touch, shaped by more than 2,500 consultation submissions. The EU chose binding law. Its AI Act requires makers of advanced models with 'systemic risk' to address cyber offences and loss of human control. In July 2026 the European Commission said it was in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic about AI-linked hacking.

Then a US state stepped in. On 18 September 2026 California Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to speed independent oversight and develop an AI 'kill switch'. It did not yet require companies to install one. November brought Australia's six mandatory protections, California's lawsuit against OpenAI, and on 18 November, proposals for mandatory standards. On 19 November Trump restated the Paris line at APEC.

analogy.text: Think of car safety. There is no single world crash-test law; each country sets its own. A carmaker selling everywhere often builds to the toughest big market's test, so one strict market lifts safety elsewhere. AI rules are heading the same way without a global treaty.
analogy.breaks: Cars are physical and checked at borders. AI is software used across borders instantly, so misuse anywhere can harm people elsewhere.

lesson.concept: How AI rules get made without a world treaty
lesson.big_idea: With no global treaty, AI rules are made place by place. A company must follow the binding rules of every place it sells in, so the strictest big markets can shape the product for everyone.

steps.title: Global deals need the big powers
steps.text: A world rule only works if the major powers sign. In February 2025, 58 countries signed the Paris AI declaration, but the US did not. On 19 November 2026 Trump said the US opposes 'globalist' AI regulation.

steps.title: Binding versus voluntary rules
steps.text: A binding rule carries penalties if broken. A voluntary one is advice. India's 2025 guidelines are voluntary and light-touch. The EU AI Act is binding: makers of advanced models with systemic risk must address cyber offences and loss of control.

steps.title: Rules stop at the border
steps.text: Each government can bind only companies working in its territory. So Australia covers Australia, the EU covers the EU, and California can propose rules such as outside testing and emergency shutdown power for California.

steps.title: One product, many rulebooks
steps.text: Separate models for every market cost more. So a company often builds one version that passes the strictest big market's rules. That is how one tough rule-maker can raise standards elsewhere.

example.setup: Imagine an AI company selling one chatbot in four places: Place A has no AI law, Place B has voluntary guidelines, Place C demands outside testing, and Place D can order emergency shutdowns.

lines.label: Place A: no law
lines.calc: Nothing required
lines.note: The company can do as it likes there.

lines.label: Place B: voluntary
lines.calc: Guidelines suggested, no penalty for ignoring them
lines.note: Good practice, not a legal duty.

lines.label: Place C: testing rule
lines.calc: Outside testers must check the model
lines.note: Binding: breaking it brings penalties.

lines.label: Place D: shutdown power
lines.calc: Government can order the model switched off
lines.note: Binding: the model needs a working off switch.

lines.label: Cheapest choice
lines.calc: Assume 2 versions cost double; build 1 meeting C and D
lines.note: One version is sold in all four places.

example.result: Places A and B get a tested model with an off switch, though their own rules never asked for it. The strictest binding rules end up shaping the product everywhere.

apply.text: So Trump's rejection does not leave AI without rules. The EU AI Act already binds advanced models. Australia announced six mandatory protections. California has proposed outside testing and shutdown power, though these are not yet law. If passed, they would act like Places C and D in our example. India, with voluntary guidelines, is like Place B.

practice.q: Suppose Place B switches to a binding rule capping AI systems that design their own successors without human input. What does the company do?
practice.answer: Step 1: Place B's rule is now binding, so the company must obey it there. Step 2: it still wants one version for all four places. Step 3: so it builds the cap into its single model. Result: the cap now reaches Places A, C and D too.

so_far.text: COP31, the 2026 UN climate summit, runs from 9 to 20 November in Antalya. Turkey hosts. Australia leads the negotiations through its minister, Chris Bowen. His first draft, on 16 November, offered two fossil-fuel options, and both could be dropped. EU envoy Wopke Hoekstra said that draft could make talks 'untenable'. A European official called the stance of a bloc including Saudi Arabia and India 'unacceptable'. Saudi Arabia and India reportedly want the UN climate science panel's next reports pushed to 2029.

what_happened.text: On 19 November, less than a day and a half before COP31's scheduled close, the presidency released a new draft cover decision. It removes every reference to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas. It also omits the fossil-fuel roadmap from Brazil's COP30 presidency. It keeps the 1.5C goal but admits warming will overshoot it. It restates tripling adaptation finance by 2035 with no dollar figure. Panama warned it would block any deal without a commitment to end fossil fuels. Bowen pledged overnight consultations.

steps.text: COP decisions need consensus, so any single country can block the whole deal.
The first draft's fossil-fuel options split the room; EU envoy Hoekstra warned it could make talks 'untenable'.
The new draft cut all fossil-fuel wording; no source names who pushed, though one analysis links it to placating Arab nations.
But Panama vows to block any deal without a fossil-fuel commitment, so the cut creates a new veto risk.
With under a day and a half left and finance unresolved, the outcome hinges on Bowen's overnight consultations.

history.text: The root is 1992, when countries adopted the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. It became the framework for every later climate negotiation. In 1997 the Kyoto Protocol gave developed countries legally binding emission cuts. It rested on 'common but differentiated responsibilities': everyone shares the problem, but those who polluted first should act first. In 2015 the Paris Agreement changed the method. Each country now sets its own targets, called nationally determined contributions, toward holding warming well below 2C and pursuing 1.5C. In 2023 COP28 in Dubai called for 'transitioning away from fossil fuels'. Even that was seen as a compromise. COP28 also put the loss and damage fund into operation. In 2025 the wording slipped back. COP30 in Belém did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, though it set a goal to triple adaptation finance by 2035. Over 80 countries backed a fossil-fuel roadmap, which Brazil's presidency pursued outside the text. So Antalya had to choose between Dubai's wording and Belém's silence. The 16 November draft offered options. The 19 November draft chose silence.

lesson.concept: How consensus decides a UN climate deal
lesson.big_idea: At a COP, a decision passes only if no country objects. So the presidency keeps rewriting until nobody blocks, and every deletion that pleases one side can provoke another.

steps.title: No vote, only consensus
steps.text: COP decisions are not taken by majority vote. They need consensus, meaning no country formally objects. So one country can block an entire deal, which is exactly what Panama has threatened at COP31.

steps.title: The presidency writes the drafts
steps.text: The summit's presidency, here Australia under Chris Bowen, drafts the text and consults countries. Its job is to find words every country can live with, not words every country loves.

steps.title: Cut what someone blocks
steps.text: When a phrase draws a firm objection, the quickest fix is to delete it or make it vaguer. Repeated many times, this pulls the text toward the weakest common ground.

steps.title: Vetoes cut both ways
steps.text: A deletion can create a new objector: a country that wanted the phrase may now block. Then the presidency must trade, offering softer wording or something the holdout values elsewhere, such as money.

steps.title: The deadline adds pressure
steps.text: A scheduled closing day pushes holdouts to compromise. But if no text satisfies every country by then, talks can run past the deadline or end without a decision.

example.setup: Imagine 10 countries must agree on one statement. Seven are flexible. Two oil producers reject any fossil-fuel wording. One country, call it Country P, insists on it.

lines.note: Two objections block it. A big majority does not matter.

lines.label: Draft 2: line cut
lines.calc: No fossil-fuel line: 9 yes, Country P objects
lines.note: Pleasing two countries created a new objector.

lines.label: Count the blockers
lines.calc: Draft 1: 2 blockers. Draft 2: 1 blocker.
lines.note: Fewer blockers, but one is still enough to stop the deal.

lines.label: Draft 3: a trade
lines.calc: Softer fossil wording plus something Country P values
lines.note: The presidency hunts for a package all 10 accept.

lines.label: The rule
lines.calc: 0 blockers = deal; 1 or more = no deal
lines.note: Consensus counts objections, not supporters.

example.result: Cutting the phrase moved the draft from two blockers to one, not to zero. Under consensus a deal needs zero blockers, so the presidency must trade or the summit fails.

apply.text: That is COP31 on 19 November. The new draft cut every fossil-fuel reference, like Draft 2 in our example. No source names who pushed; one analysis links it to placating Arab nations. But Panama, like Country P, says it will block any deal without a fossil-fuel commitment. Bowen's overnight consultations are the search for a Draft 3 with zero blockers.

practice.q: Suppose Draft 3 restores 'transitioning away from fossil fuels'. Country P and one oil producer accept, but the other oil producer still objects. Is there a deal?
practice.answer: Count the blockers. Seven flexible countries: no objection. Country P and one oil producer: no objection. The other oil producer: objects. That is 1 blocker. Consensus needs 0, so there is no deal yet. The presidency must win over that last producer with new wording or a trade elsewhere.

scenes.speak: अब players की बात। Chris Bowen drafts लिखते हैं और Australia की तरफ़ से talks lead करते हैं। EU climate envoy Wopke Hoekstra ने पहले draft को criticise किया। Panama veto की धमकी दे रहा है। India के environment minister, Bhupender Yadav, ने अभी तय नहीं किया है कि electrification target को support करें या नहीं।

scenes.say: Ab numbers. Developing countries ne adaptation ke liye kam se kam 120 billion dollar maange, yaani climate ke nuksaan se nipatne mein madad. Naye draft mein na koi dollar figure hai, na koi baseline. Woh bas 2035 tak adaptation ka paisa teen guna karne ki baat dohrata hai.
scenes.speak: अब numbers। Developing countries ने adaptation के लिए कम से कम 120 billion dollar माँगे, यानी climate के नुक़सान से निपटने में मदद। नए draft में न कोई dollar figure है, न कोई baseline। वो बस 2035 तक adaptation का पैसा तीन गुना करने की बात दोहराता है।

scenes.say: Iski jagah, yeh ek Antalya to Addis Ababa roadmap propose karta hai, jo agle summit par, Ethiopia mein, khatam hoga. Aur ek UN finance committee se baseline options par report maangta hai. Turkey ka 2035 ke liye 35 percent electrification target bana rehta hai. Saath hi 2030 tak renewable power teen guna aur saalana efficiency gains double karne ki maang hai.
scenes.speak: इसकी जगह, ये एक Antalya to Addis Ababa roadmap propose करता है, जो अगले summit पर, Ethiopia में, ख़त्म होगा। और एक UN finance committee से baseline options पर report माँगता है। Turkey का 2035 के लिए 35 percent electrification target बना रहता है। साथ ही 2030 तक renewable power तीन गुना और सालाना efficiency gains double करने की माँग है।

scenes.say: Hall ke bahar, NPR ne 19 November ko report kiya ki China ke emissions plateau par aa gaye hain aur shayad gir bhi rahe hain. Carbon Brief ne February 2026 mein China ka 2025 ka badlaav lagbhag minus zero point three percent bataya. Ek chhota sa rebound ise palat sakta hai.
scenes.speak: Hall के बाहर, NPR ने 19 November को report किया कि China के emissions plateau पर आ गए हैं और शायद गिर भी रहे हैं। Carbon Brief ने February 2026 में China का 2025 का बदलाव लगभग minus zero point three percent बताया। एक छोटा सा rebound इसे पलट सकता है।

scenes.say: Ab is sab ke peeche ka ek idea: consensus. Faisla tabhi paas hota hai jab koi desh objection na kare. Presidency drafts likhti hai, aise shabd dhoondhte hue jinke saath sab reh sakein. Jab kisi phrase par pakka objection aata hai, toh sabse jaldi fix hai use kaat dena ya aur vague bana dena.
scenes.speak: अब इस सब के पीछे का एक idea: consensus। फ़ैसला तभी पास होता है जब कोई देश objection न करे। Presidency drafts लिखती है, ऐसे शब्द ढूँढते हुए जिनके साथ सब रह सकें। जब किसी phrase पर पक्का objection आता है, तो सबसे जल्दी fix है उसे काट देना या और vague बना देना।

scenes.say: Lekin veto dono taraf chalta hai. Kuch hatane se naya objector khada ho sakta hai. Phir presidency ko trade karna padta hai, naram wording dekar ya kuch aur, jaise paisa. Sochiye, flatmates house rules likh rahe hain aur koi bhi veto kar sakta hai. Agar deadline tak kuch bhi sabko satisfy nahi karta, toh talks overrun ho sakti hain ya bina faisle ke khatam ho sakti hain.
scenes.image: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
scenes.speak: लेकिन veto दोनों तरफ़ चलता है। कुछ हटाने से नया objector खड़ा हो सकता है। फिर presidency को trade करना पड़ता है, नरम wording देकर या कुछ और, जैसे पैसा। सोचिए, flatmates house rules लिख रहे हैं और कोई भी veto कर सकता है। अगर deadline तक कुछ भी सबको satisfy नहीं करता, तो talks overrun हो सकती हैं या बिना फ़ैसले के ख़त्म हो सकती हैं।

scenes.say: Maan lijiye 10 desh hain. 7 flexible hain. 2 oil producers fossil-fuel wording reject karte hain. Aur Country P use zaroor chahta hai. Pehla draft kehta hai, fossil fuels phase out karo: 8 haan, 2 objection. Blocked. Doosra draft woh line kaat deta hai: 9 haan, lekin Country P objection karta hai. Phir bhi blocked. 2 blockers 1 ban gaye. Deal ke liye chahiye zero.
scenes.speak: मान लीजिए 10 देश हैं। 7 flexible हैं। 2 oil producers fossil-fuel wording reject करते हैं। और Country P उसे ज़रूर चाहता है। पहला draft कहता है, fossil fuels phase out करो: 8 हाँ, 2 objection। Blocked। दूसरा draft वो line काट देता है: 9 हाँ, लेकिन Country P objection करता है। फिर भी blocked। 2 blockers 1 बन गए। Deal के लिए चाहिए zero।

scenes.say: Toh teesra draft ek trade hona chahiye, shayad thodi naram fossil-fuel wording, plus kuch aisa jo Country P ke liye maayne rakhe. Antalya mein, 19 November ka text doosra draft hai. Panama hai Country P. Aur Bowen ki raat bhar ki consultations, teesre draft ki talaash hain.
scenes.speak: तो तीसरा draft एक trade होना चाहिए, शायद थोड़ी नरम fossil-fuel wording, plus कुछ ऐसा जो Country P के लिए मायने रखे। Antalya में, 19 November का text दूसरा draft है। Panama है Country P। और Bowen की रात भर की consultations, तीसरे draft की तलाश हैं।

scenes.say: Kaun kya keh raha hai? Panama: fossil-fuel commitment nahi, toh deal nahi, aur isme oil production par cap bhi shaamil hai. India ke Yadav chahte hain ki electrification target negotiated text ke bahar rahe, aur voluntary pledges alag rahein. Aur EU envoy Wopke Hoekstra ne warning di thi ki pehla draft, apne droppable fossil-fuel options ke saath, talks ko untenable bana sakta hai.
scenes.speak: कौन क्या कह रहा है? Panama: fossil-fuel commitment नहीं, तो deal नहीं, और इसमें oil production पर cap भी शामिल है। India के Yadav चाहते हैं कि electrification target negotiated text के बाहर रहे, और voluntary pledges अलग रहें। और EU envoy Wopke Hoekstra ने warning दी थी कि पहला draft, अपने droppable fossil-fuel options के साथ, talks को untenable बना सकता है।

views.view: No fossil-fuel commitment, no deal; wants an oil production cap
Electrification target belongs outside the negotiated text
First draft could make the talks 'untenable'

scenes.say: Ek aam galti: yeh sochna ki aisi deals majority vote se paas hoti hain. Asal mein, inhe consensus chahiye. Panama jaisa ek desh sab kuch block kar sakta hai.
scenes.speak: एक आम ग़लती: ये सोचना कि ऐसी deals majority vote से पास होती हैं। असल में, इन्हें consensus चाहिए। Panama जैसा एक देश सब कुछ block कर सकता है।

scenes.say: India ke liye iska matlab kya hai? Asli baat yeh hai ki India kis cheez par sign kar sakta hai. India 35 percent electrification target ko negotiated text mein daalne ko oppose karta hai. Minister Yadav ne abhi tay nahi kiya ki ise endorse karein ya nahi. Reports ke mutabik India aur Saudi Arabia chahte hain ki agli UN climate science reports 2029 tak tal di jayein. Fossil-fuel wording par India ki formal position pata nahi hai.
scenes.speak: India के लिए इसका मतलब क्या है? असली बात ये है कि India किस चीज़ पर sign कर सकता है। India 35 percent electrification target को negotiated text में डालने को oppose करता है। Minister Yadav ने अभी तय नहीं किया कि इसे endorse करें या नहीं। Reports के मुताबिक़ India और Saudi Arabia चाहते हैं कि अगली UN climate science reports 2029 तक टाल दी जाएँ। Fossil-fuel wording पर India की formal position पता नहीं है।

scenes.say: Ab kya dekhna hai. Summit 20 November ko close hona scheduled hai. Kya fossil-fuel wording wapas aayegi? Kya Panama block karega? Kya talks overrun hongi? Abhi tak koi source nahi batata. China ke liye, March 2027 mein uska five-year plan dekhiye.
scenes.speak: अब क्या देखना है। Summit 20 November को close होना scheduled है। क्या fossil-fuel wording वापस आएगी? क्या Panama block करेगा? क्या talks overrun होंगी? अभी तक कोई source नहीं बताता। China के लिए, March 2027 में उसका five-year plan देखिए।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. Ek desh climate deal block kar sakta hai, kyunki faisle consensus se hote hain. 19 November ke draft ne saari fossil-fuel wording hata di, aur Panama veto ki dhamki de raha hai. Dekhiye ki woh wording wapas aati hai ya nahi, aur summit 20 November ko khatam hota hai ya overrun karta hai.
scenes.image: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। एक देश climate deal block कर सकता है, क्योंकि फ़ैसले consensus से होते हैं। 19 November के draft ने सारी fossil-fuel wording हटा दी, और Panama veto की धमकी दे रहा है। देखिए कि वो wording वापस आती है या नहीं, और summit 20 November को ख़त्म होता है या overrun करता है।
